teaser: A company that makes rooftop air conditioners saw revenue jump 84 percent in a year. Why?
fallbackLine: At leisure, osmanthus blossoms fall; in the still night, the spring mountain lies empty.

pieces.title: The firing squad had already raised its rifles; only then did the pardon arrive: Dostoevsky
pieces.hook: He turned the most unbearable experience into a question worth asking: he survived the execution ground and hard labor, and what he wrote was not “how miserable I am,” but…
pieces.takeaway: He turned the most unbearable experience into a question worth asking: he survived the execution ground and hard labor, and what he wrote was not “how miserable I am,” but what choices a person still makes at the limit.
pieces.imageAlt: Portrait of Dostoevsky painted by Perov
pieces.imageCredit: Vasily Perov · public domain, Wikimedia Commons

parts: Fyodor Mikhailovich Dostoevsky (1821–1881) was a Russian writer. By the Gregorian calendar, today is the 205th anniversary of his birth: on 11 November 1821 (30 October in the Julian calendar), he was born in the doctors’ quarters of a hospital for the poor in Moscow, the second of seven children.

paras.lead: A literary young man in an engineering school
parts: In 1838 he entered the Military Engineering School in St. Petersburg. His father died the following year; the official account was that he had been killed by serfs, a claim that has been disputed ever since. After graduating he served briefly as a military engineer, then resigned to write full time.

In 1846 his novella Poor Folk was published. The critic Vissarion Belinsky praised it, and Dostoevsky became famous almost overnight. From 1847 he attended meetings of the Petrashevsky circle, where banned social ideas and serfdom were discussed. In April 1849 (Julian calendar) he was arrested and held in the Peter and Paul Fortress.

On 22 December of the same year (Julian calendar), he and his fellow prisoners were taken to Semyonovsky Square. The first three men had already been tied to stakes, and the firing squad raised its rifles—only then did a messenger arrive, announcing that the tsar had commuted the sentence to hard labor. One of the condemned could not bear the spectacle and suffered a mental collapse.
Two days later, Dostoevsky was exiled to Siberia.

From 1850 to 1854 he served hard labor in the prison at Omsk, confined with serious criminals. He later turned that experience into Notes from a Dead House. After his release he was drafted into the army and posted as a private to Semipalatinsk (now Semey, Kazakhstan).
There he married the widow Maria Isaeva. Epilepsy was formally diagnosed, though the symptoms had already been present.

In 1859 he was allowed to return to St. Petersburg. With his brother Mikhail he founded, one after the other, the magazines Vremya (Time) and Epokha (The Epoch), which published Notes from a Dead House and other work. The magazines were first banned, then closed because of money troubles. In 1864 his wife and his brother died in succession, and his debts grew heavier.

paras.lead: A novel dictated in twenty-six days
parts: In 1866, to meet a harsh publishing contract, he hired Anna Snitkina, who had just finished stenography school, to take dictation, and completed The Gambler in 26 days. Crime and Punishment appeared in the same year. On 15 February 1867 (Julian calendar), at the age of 45, he married Anna, who was 25 years younger than he was.

After the wedding they spent four years in Europe. He went repeatedly to Germany to play roulette and lost everything; their first daughter, Sonya, died in infancy in Geneva. After returning to Russia in 1871, he stopped gambling and left the household and his publishing affairs to Anna.

Anna set about sorting out contracts and royalties and ran the publication of his books; the family’s finances gradually steadied. Some accounts regard her as one of the first women in Russia to manage a publishing business of her own.

He later wrote Demons, and in 1880 finished The Brothers Karamazov, which he dedicated to Anna. That same year he delivered a speech at the Pushkin memorial celebrations in Moscow, and his reputation reached its height. On 9 February 1881 (Gregorian calendar; 28 January in the Julian calendar) he died in St. Petersburg of a pulmonary hemorrhage, at the age of 59.
Crowds gathered along the funeral route. Later accounts disagree about the numbers, with estimates ranging from “tens of thousands” to “about a hundred thousand.”

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Dostoevsky himself | View: the inner life is more worth questioning than the slogans of a system. ; Interest: turning what he had lived through into books, while also paying off debts and supporting a family. ; Worry: books banned, creditors at the door, epileptic seizures. ; Basis: Notes from a Dead House and Crime and Punishment; after 1871 he left the finances to Anna.

The tsarist authorities | View: a gathering to talk about ideas could also become subversion. ; Interest: keeping order and imperial power. ; Worry: Western European ideas spreading into the army and among the young. ; Basis: the arrest of the Petrashevsky circle; commuting a mock execution to hard labor was one of the punishments then used against political prisoners.

Radical critics and later revolutionaries | View: literature should help drive change. ; Interest: spreading new ideas through society. ; Worry: his later turn toward a more conservative stance. ; Basis: early praise from Belinsky; Demons is sharply critical of revolutionary conspiracy.

Anna | View: even genius needs a ledger and a contract. ; Interest: a stable household, and work that could keep being published. ; Worry: gambling and creditors dragging the family down again. ; Basis: she took dictation, managed publishing, and preserved a large body of manuscripts and letters.

Later readers and scholars | View: he is one of the key sources of the modern novel, but he should not be turned into a saint. ; Interest: how to make sense of crime, punishment, and faith. ; Worry: taking a character’s extreme psychology as the author’s whole argument. ; Basis: the books are still translated and adapted around the world; details such as the size of the funeral crowd are told differently.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: The authorities tried to break him with the threat of death, and in doing so handed the rest of his life the question of how a person lives at the limit.
A harsh publishing contract forced The Gambler into being, and also brought Anna into his life.
He wrote about the poor and about guilt, yet for years he was himself bound by debt and gambling—his life and his themes were tangled together.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: He asked about free will and salvation, but did not offer an answer everyone could accept; that is why these books are still opened.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: Whether his father was killed by serfs is still debated among historians.
Figures for the funeral crowd come from observations at the time and from later recollections, and the estimates vary widely.
The phrase “Russia’s first publishing house run by a woman” is a later summary of Anna’s work, and should not be treated as a precise “first.”

pieces.title: How a piece of paper with no value of its own became money people would accept: a thousand years of paper currency
pieces.short: A thousand years of paper money
pieces.hook: A piece of iron cash was heavy and clumsy. When merchants went out to trade, they had to haul it by cart.
pieces.imageAlt: A Yuan-dynasty Zhiyuan banknote and its printing plate

parts: A piece of iron cash was heavy and clumsy. When merchants went out to trade, they had to haul it by cart. A thousand years ago, people in Sichuan came up with a method: write the amount on paper, and let the paper stand for money. The question is—if anyone can print it, is that paper still money?

In the early Northern Song, iron cash circulated in what is now Sichuan, and it was awkward to use. Private jiaozi shops appeared: a customer deposited iron coins, and the shop issued a voucher on mulberry paper—a “private jiaozi.” During the reign of Emperor Zhenzong, Zhang Yong, the prefect of Yizhou, pushed a plan in which sixteen wealthy merchant houses jointly guaranteed the notes and issued them on uniform paper and in a uniform format.
Some of the shops could not honor the notes. The market was shaken, and private jiaozi were banned for a time.

After the ban, trade became inconvenient again. Officials asked that the right to issue the notes be taken over by the government. On the 28th day of the 11th month of the first year of Tiansheng—12 January 1024 in the Gregorian calendar—the court established a Jiaozi Office in Yizhou; in April of the following year, the first series of official jiaozi was issued.
The China Numismatic Society and other institutions treat that day as the founding date of the world’s earliest official paper-money authority.

According to Yi Gang, president of the China Society for Finance and Banking and a former governor of the central bank, each series of official jiaozi was capped at 1.25 million guan, with a reserve of about 360,000 guan in iron cash, a reserve ratio of roughly 28 percent. A series lasted three years; when it expired, old notes were exchanged for new ones. The paper itself had no value. Its value rested on the expectation that it could be redeemed for iron cash, and on the rules that limited how much could be issued.

After official jiaozi had circulated for some eighty years, fiscal and military pressure grew, and over-issue brought depreciation. Around 1107, jiaozi were renamed qianyin. In the Southern Song, huizi circulated more widely, almost becoming legal tender in the southeast, and came closer to an inconvertible state-credit currency.

The Yuan dynasty pushed paper money across the country; The Travels of Marco Polo described payment with paper in China. Early Ming treasure notes, the Da Ming Baochao, later depreciated just as badly. After the Single Whip reform in the Wanli period, silver rose in importance, and this centuries-long experiment with paper money largely came to an end.

paras.lead: Europe was more than six hundred years later
parts: In 1661, Stockholm Banco, founded by Johan Palmstruch, issued Europe’s first circulating banknotes, meant to replace extremely heavy copper coins. The bank over-issued, ran into trouble around 1668, Palmstruch was convicted, and the Swedish Riksdag for a time forbade any further issue of paper money.

The Bank of England was founded in 1694, and banknotes gradually became a more stable institution. From 1696, the Bank of Scotland’s note issue has lasted an exceptionally long time, and is often called one of the longest-running banknote issues anywhere.

paras.lead: The promise to redeem is broken
parts: In the modern era, paper money was long tied to gold and silver. In August 1971, the United States ended the convertibility of the dollar into gold, and the Bretton Woods system collapsed. Major economies then entered the era of fiat money: banknotes and electronic bookkeeping rest on state credit and on the force of law.
The old problems of over-issue and inflation have not gone away.

The paper is still there; it is used less and less. Today most payments have become numbers on a card, a phone, or an account, and many central banks are also testing digital currencies. But the logic of “why people will accept a voucher that has no value of its own” has not changed: issuance has to be limited, and someone has to believe the system will still be there tomorrow.

blocks.title: Stockholm Banco: the lesson of Europe’s first paper money
blocks.text: The “credit notes” it issued were meant to replace heavy copper plates, and they were popular; but the bank printed too many, could not redeem them, and within a few years was in trouble. The founder was convicted. It was almost the same script as the early redemption crisis of Sichuan jiaozi.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Merchants and jiaozi shops | View: iron cash is too heavy; a light payment voucher is needed. ; Interest: expanding trade, and the convenience of exchange and safekeeping. ; Worry: rivals issuing notes too freely, and being unable to redeem them. ; Basis: even a joint guarantee by sixteen houses still produced a redemption crisis, and private jiaozi were banned for a time.

The government | View: the right to issue should belong to the authorities, serving both the public and the treasury. ; Interest: a way to raise funds besides minting coin, and control over the market. ; Worry: a collapse of convertibility, and the unrest that would follow. ; Basis: the Jiaozi Office was set up in 1024; later over-issue led to depreciation.

Ordinary holders and traveling traders | View: as long as it can be spent and exchanged, paper is more convenient than iron cash. ; Interest: lower costs of carrying and transacting. ; Worry: depreciation, counterfeits, and losses when notes are exchanged at the end of a series. ; Basis: in periods of over-issue, prices rose and notes traded at a discount.

Modern banks and central banks | View: unified issue, a reserve system, and clearing are what make paper money stable. ; Interest: seigniorage, and room for monetary policy. ; Worry: runs, and fiscal pressure to print. ; Basis: the failure of Stockholm Banco; the Bank of England and others gradually built stricter rules for issue.

Today’s payment firms and central-bank digital currencies | View: less paper can be printed, but bookkeeping still needs an authority. ; Interest: payment efficiency, data, and monetary sovereignty. ; Worry: privacy, runs on digital channels, and credit being overstretched. ; Basis: the spread of electronic payments; many countries are testing central-bank digital currencies.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: Convenience and restraint are in tension: the easier it is to issue, the smoother trade becomes, and the wider the door to depreciation also swings.
Private actors invented the voucher first. Once the government took over the right to issue, it could police the market—or over-issue for fiscal needs.
Gold once stood behind paper money. After the gold standard ended, restraint has rested more on institutions and on expectations.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: Technology has changed over a thousand years, from mulberry paper to electronic accounts. The hard part is still the same sentence: who will guarantee that this “voucher” will not be printed past its limit.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: No generally accepted physical Northern Song jiaozi has yet been found; early designs are known mostly from written sources.
Whether jiaozi began as deposit receipts is still a point some scholars think needs more research.
Marco Polo’s account helped Europeans learn about Chinese paper money, but it should not be inflated into a claim that he “directly taught Europe how to print banknotes.”

pieces.title: A rooftop-air-conditioner company saw revenue jump 84 percent in a year: AAON is making money cooling AI
pieces.hook: After the U.S. market closed on 9 November, the American HVAC company AAON reported its third quarter (through September…
pieces.event: Third-quarter results after the close on 2026-11-09 (U.S. Eastern time); the close on 11-10 was up 19.31 percent
pieces.imageAlt: Cooling towers on the roof of a data center

parts: After the U.S. market closed on 9 November, the American HVAC company AAON reported third-quarter results (through 30 September): revenue of $707.4 million, up 84.1 percent from a year earlier, a company record. The next day (10 November) the shares closed up 19.31 percent at $75.01, on about four times the usual volume.

AAON was founded in 1988 in Oklahoma and the next year moved into a plant in Tulsa, where it launched rooftop heating-and-cooling units—the big square metal boxes on the roofs of malls and warehouses. It listed on Nasdaq in 1993, and for decades sold mainly to commercial buildings.

In December 2021, AAON acquired Oregon-based BASX for $100 million up front, plus up to $80 million more in stock, payable in installments if performance targets were met. BASX specializes in custom cooling equipment for large data centers; it was then expected to do about $70 million in revenue for the year.
In its announcement, AAON said the deal let the company “immediately enter” the data-center and clean-room markets, which it had barely touched before.

Five years later, the BASX brand alone sold $397.2 million this quarter, up 218.3 percent; the original AAON brand sold $310.2 million, up 19.6 percent. In other words, the half that depends on data centers is already larger than the half that sells building air-conditioning.

The chips that train and run AI are densely packed and run hot, and data centers increasingly rely on liquid cooling: fluid carries heat away directly from the racks. According to the trade publication HeatAirNews, citing the results, BASX’s liquid-cooling products sold $165.5 million this quarter, up 255.6 percent.

Operating income was $100 million, up 129.3 percent. Earnings per share were $0.83, compared with $0.37 a year earlier, and above analysts’ expectations of about $0.56. Full-year revenue-growth guidance was raised from 55–60 percent to 72–75 percent.
As of the end of September, the backlog was $1.85 billion, up 40.5 percent, of which BASX accounted for $1.36 billion.

paras.lead: The bad news in the same report
parts: The company admitted that the books for the first two quarters had been wrong: percentage-of-completion revenue recognition and the amortization of software subscription costs were both flawed. The first- and second-quarter statements have to be restated, and management concluded that internal control over financial reporting had a “material weakness.” After the restatement, first-half revenue was $10.7 million higher and earnings per share $0.09 higher; looking at the first quarter alone, though, net income was $3.4 million lower.

paras.lead: The backlog fell from the prior quarter
parts: The backlog was 5.9 percent lower than at the end of June. The company’s explanation is that factory capacity has come online, so orders are turning into revenue faster, while the timing of large BASX awards has always been uneven.

paras.lead: Why the stock jumped so far
parts: One backdrop is a low base: even after the rally, the shares were still about half their 52-week high of $150.46, and down about 40 percent over the past year (Stocktreats data). On 4 November, the week before the results, they had already fallen 15.7 percent in a single day. Better-than-expected revenue and raised guidance landed right on that low point.

First, the “selling shovels” business: in the AI boom, the companies making money are not only those that build chips and models, but also older industries that power and cool the machine rooms. Second, the judgment in an acquisition: a small company bought for $100 million now supports half of revenue.

Third, read the whole report: the restatement and the material weakness sitting next to the good numbers are information too. The inferences above are based on public filings and are not investment advice.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: AAON management | View: data-center demand is strong, and the expanded plants are turning orders into revenue. ; Interest: revenue growth, market share, and a repair of the valuation. ; Worry: the restatement damaging trust; the uneven timing of large awards. ; Basis: the earnings release: full-year guidance raised, with orders still expected to be strong in the fourth quarter and into 2027; a material weakness was also disclosed and is being remediated.

Data-center customers (hyperscale cloud firms and others) | View: they need cooling systems that can be delivered quickly and customized for high-density racks. ; Interest: delivery speed, energy efficiency, and liquid-cooling capability. ; Worry: suppliers’ capacity not keeping up, and lead times stretching. ; Basis: the release said growth in BASX orders reflects “customers’ continued investment in data-center infrastructure”; the company website says BASX has delivered 80 megawatts of cooling in six months.

Investors | View: revenue and guidance that beat expectations deserve a new price. ; Interest: whether the growth lasts, and the valuation. ; Worry: accounting problems recurring; the AI investment cycle cooling. ; Basis: the shares rose 19.31 percent on 11-10, on about four times usual volume; they were still about half the 52-week high.

Auditors and regulators | View: published figures have to be reliable; if they are wrong, they must be corrected in public. ; Interest: the credibility of the financials, and investor protection. ; Worry: a material weakness not being remedied in time. ; Basis: the 8-K filing: the first- and second-quarter statements “should no longer be relied upon”; the audit committee has discussed the matter with the auditor, Grant Thornton.

The traditional building-HVAC business and its customers | View: the older business is still growing, and lead times are shortening. ; Interest: a steady stream of commercial-building orders. ; Worry: company resources tilting toward data centers; a soft end market. ; Basis: the release: AAON-brand orders were up 18 percent year on year, but the “end-market environment is soft,” and orders were down 7.6 percent from the prior quarter.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: Data-center orders have pushed revenue up, and have also made the company more dependent on the investment cycle of a few large customers—the 5.9 percent quarter-on-quarter drop in the backlog is a shadow of that volatility.
Expansion has made delivery faster, but it has also made revenue recognition more complicated; this restatement landed precisely on percentage-of-completion accounting.
Investors rewarded the growth with the share price, but the result of remedying the “material weakness” will have to wait for later reports to be tested.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: How long the boom in AI data-center construction lasts will decide whether BASX’s high growth can continue; neither the company nor investors can know that in advance.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: The past year’s decline and the 52-week high come from a third-party market-data site; sources differ slightly.
The sales figure for liquid-cooling products comes from a trade publication’s account of the filings.
The “selling shovels” analogy is a way of describing the business model; it is not the company’s own phrase.

pieces.title: A member of the same party moves to impeach his own party’s secretary: the House votes on the Hegseth case
pieces.short: The House votes on Hegseth’s impeachment
pieces.hook: On 9 November, Representative Thomas Massie, a Republican from Kentucky, introduced a resolution in the House to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth for “high crimes and…
pieces.event: Impeachment resolution introduced on 11-09; House procedural vote on the evening of 11-10 (U.S. Eastern time)
pieces.imageAlt: The chamber of the U.S. House of Representatives
pieces.imageCredit: U.S. House of Representatives / Office of the Speaker · public domain, Wikimedia Commons

parts: On 9 November, Representative Thomas Massie, a Republican from Kentucky, introduced a resolution in the House to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth for “high crimes and misdemeanors.” The resolution runs to 34 pages and eight articles; at its core is the charge that he waged war on Iran without authorization from Congress.

Massie raised it as a question of the privileges of the House, which means the leadership must schedule a vote within two legislative days. The majority can first move to “table” the resolution or refer it to committee—that takes only a simple majority, and if it passes, the impeachment effort stops at the door.

The House had been due to take that procedural vote at 5:30 p.m. Eastern time on 10 November (6:30 a.m. on the 11th, Beijing time). Before the vote, the clerk read all of the articles of impeachment on the floor.

The first four all concern Iran: waging war without authorization; ignoring a congressional resolution calling for a halt to the fighting; exceeding the statutory 60-day limit on the use of force (Massie says the deadline was 1 May); and disregarding civilian casualties, including an attack on an Iranian primary school in February. The remaining four are: strikes on drug-running boats in the Caribbean that killed at least 243 people; retaliation over remarks by Senator Mark Kelly; the arrest of Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro; and the 2025 air strikes on Yemen’s Houthis.

Massie had already introduced articles in September; House leadership adjourned early then, pushing a vote into November. After the midterm elections on 3 November, Democrats won both chambers of the next Congress. Roll Call reported that voters’ ballots were driven in large part by discontent over the war with Iran and the higher prices it helped push up.
Massie himself lost his primary to a Trump-backed challenger, and will leave office in January.

On 10 November, Hegseth held his first Pentagon press conference in six months. He called the impeachment a “political stunt” and a “farce,” said every military operation had been “lawful,” and called Massie a “disgruntled, defeated member.” Trump graded him “A PLUS PLUS” and called Massie a “loser through and through.”

House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said he was a “solid yes.” Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said Hegseth was “completely unfit” to lead the Pentagon. On the Republican side, Speaker Mike Johnson said “we have the votes” to block it. Vice President JD Vance blamed the midterm losses on the war, yet called the charge that Hegseth had committed an impeachable offense “ridiculous.” Republican senator Ted Cruz had earlier said a House impeachment was “highly likely.”

Impeachment in the House requires only a simple majority; a Senate trial follows, and conviction and removal require a two-thirds vote. Massie says the articles would carry over into the next Congress, when Democrats will control the Senate. NBC noted that if the articles pass, he would be the first sitting defense (or war) secretary impeached in about 150 years.

For Republicans, this is a test of position after an election loss: every vote will be recorded, and members who still have to face voters in 2028 will weigh it carefully. For the relationship between the executive and the legislature, it puts back on the table the question of whether a president can wage a prolonged war without authorization from Congress.

Roll Call, citing the Congressional Research Service, noted that recent impeachment efforts pushed directly as questions of privilege have not passed, and that officials who were impeached had almost always been investigated first.

One is to call it simply “partisan fighting”—the sponsor himself is a Republican. A second is to treat the procedural vote as impeachment itself: whether a motion to table passes is not the same thing as “Hegseth has been impeached.” A third is to equate “impeached” with “removed from office”—removal requires two-thirds of the Senate.
A fourth is to look only at casualty figures from one side. Some of the events in the articles, the Pentagon says, are still under investigation and have not been acknowledged as its responsibility.

critical.label: Another way to see it
items: Massie (the sponsor, a Republican) | View: the question is not whether the war was right, but whether the secretary committed an impeachable offense—“the answer is yes, eight times.” ; Interest: Congress’s power to declare war, and the War Powers Resolution. ; Worry: Republican colleagues staying silent out of loyalty to the president. ; Basis: CBS quoted his posts on X; in a Roll Call interview he said he wanted the president “to see one of his own horses shot out from under him.”

Hegseth and the White House | View: the military operations were all lawful; the impeachment is a political stunt. ; Interest: the executive’s power to use force, and continuity of policy. ; Worry: the case reaching a Senate trial and constraining war decisions. ; Basis: the Pentagon press conference (NBC, BBC); Trump called his performance “A PLUS PLUS”; the White House said the president, as commander-in-chief, has the authority to use force.

Republican leadership and most Republican members | View: a policy disagreement is not an impeachable crime. ; Interest: party unity, and the relationship with the president. ; Worry: voters holding them to account after the election loss; departing members skipping the vote. ; Basis: Speaker Johnson said “we have the votes”; Vance called the charge “ridiculous”; Roll Call analyzed that departing members might be absent.

Democrats | View: Hegseth abused his power and dragged the country into a costly war. ; Interest: assigning responsibility for the war, and paving the way for oversight once they control Congress next year. ; Worry: the impeachment being blocked by a procedural motion. ; Basis: Jeffries’s “solid yes”; Schumer’s “completely unfit”; Representative Adam Smith predicted it would pass (as quoted by Roll Call).

Service members, federal civilian employees, and voters | View: concern about the risks of war, casualties, and the cost of living. ; Interest: physical safety, job rights, and prices. ; Worry: the war continuing, and responsibility remaining unclear. ; Basis: AFGE, a union representing about 820,000 federal employees, wrote to House members asking them to vote yes (Roll Call); the midterm results have been widely read as a rebuke of the war.

critical.label: Constraints and exchanges
items: Massie used a “question of privilege” to force the leadership to take a position within two days; the leadership can use a procedural motion to avoid a vote on impeachment itself—both sides are fighting over what is actually being voted on.
Members who have lost or are retiring feel less pressure to run again, but may also simply stay away; turnout itself can change the result.
The White House and the vice president have separated the war from the man: they admit the war hurt them at the polls, but do not accept that the secretary is guilty.

critical.label: Where it gets stuck
items: How long a president may fight a war without authorization from Congress has long been legally contested: Congress regards the War Powers Resolution as binding; administrations have often disagreed. The impeachment case presses that old question onto one person.

critical.label: Where the evidence is thin
items: At the time of writing (the morning of the 11th, Beijing time), the result of the House procedural vote had not yet been announced; the official tally is the one that counts.
Some of the casualty figures in the articles come from the sponsor; the Pentagon says the incidents are still under investigation and has not accepted responsibility.
That “the articles can carry over into the next Congress” is Massie’s claim, and it is procedurally disputed.
